name: Noether's Theorem
statement: Every continuous symmetry of a physical system yields a conserved quantity.
meaning: For any system describable by an action, each continuous symmetry (a smooth transformation that leaves the action unchanged) corresponds to a quantity that stays constant in time. Symmetries and conservation laws are two sides of one coin: if the laws of physics do not change over time, energy is conserved; if they are the same everywhere in space, momentum is conserved; if they are the same in every direction, angular momentum is conserved.
mechanism: A system is described by an action, the integral over time of a Lagrangian. A continuous symmetry is a transformation depending smoothly on a parameter that leaves the action invariant. Noether's procedure constructs, from each such symmetry, an explicit conserved current whose divergence vanishes whenever the equations of motion hold; integrating it gives a conserved charge. So a Lagrangian with no explicit time dependence conserves energy, and an ignorable coordinate conserves its conjugate momentum.

examples.text: Because the laws of physics do not change from one moment to the next, time-translation symmetry, energy is conserved; this is the deep reason behind the conservation of energy.
Because the laws are the same at every location, spatial-translation symmetry, total linear momentum is conserved.
Because the laws are the same in every orientation, rotational symmetry, angular momentum is conserved; and the phase symmetry of a charged field yields conservation of electric charge.

variants.name: Noether's second theorem
variants.text: The companion result for local, gauge symmetries parametrised by arbitrary functions, which yields identities among the equations of motion rather than ordinary conservation laws: the reason energy in general relativity is subtle.

variants.name: Gauge symmetry and charge
variants.text: The application to the phase symmetries underlying electromagnetism and the Standard Model, where local invariance underpins the conservation of charge.

whyItMatters: It unified the great conservation laws (energy, momentum, angular momentum, charge) as consequences of symmetry, transforming how physicists understand why anything is conserved at all. It is a cornerstone of classical mechanics, field theory, quantum field theory, and the Standard Model, and one of the most profound results in mathematical physics.

working.lead: Look for the symmetry behind a conservation law
working.text: when a quantity is conserved, seek the continuous symmetry that produces it, and vice versa.

working.lead: Read invariance as a conserved charge
working.text: if the action is unchanged by a smooth transformation, expect a corresponding quantity to be constant in time.
treat global symmetries as giving conservation laws and local gauge symmetries as giving identities, per the two theorems.

limits: It applies only to continuous, differentiable symmetries; discrete symmetries like parity or reflection yield no Noether current. It requires a system derivable from an action, so purely dissipative systems with friction need not obey the corresponding conservation law even when a symmetry is present. And in general relativity, whose diffeomorphism invariance is a local symmetry, energy-momentum conservation becomes subtle and only globally well-defined under special conditions: the very problem that motivated the theorem.
misreadings: It is not a claim that everything is conserved, only quantities tied to a continuous symmetry are, and only for systems with an action. And the popular version often conflates the two theorems: global symmetries give conservation laws, while local gauge symmetries give identities among the equations of motion.
origin: Proved by the German mathematician Emmy Noether in 'Invariante Variationsprobleme' (1918), work she undertook at Gottingen amid the general-relativity energy problem posed by Hilbert and Klein, and despite being barred, as a woman, from a regular faculty post until 1919.
